claims.text: The initial HEA multilayer coating has highly coherent interfaces between adjacent layers.
A thin tungsten interlayer is inserted between the HEA layers.
Adding a tungsten interlayer shifts the dominant creep mechanism from diffusion-mediated creep at lower homologous temperatures to dislocation-mediated creep at higher temperatures.
Diffusion is active below approximately 0.4 Tm in the proposed HEA multilayers.
Dislocation activity increases at approximately 0.5–0.6 Tm in the proposed HEA multilayers.
Tungsten has a high melting point and low diffusivity.
The tungsten interlayer forms a stable, coherent transition layer.
The tungsten transition layer impedes atomic diffusion across the multilayer interfaces.
At elevated temperatures, the tungsten interlayer promotes dislocation nucleation and glide.
At lower temperatures, creep in the multilayer is controlled by atomic diffusion across interfaces.
As temperature increases, tungsten-mediated maintenance of interface coherency limits diffusional creep.
Suppression of diffusion by the coherent tungsten interlayer encourages dislocation-mediated plasticity.
Tungsten-modified multilayers will exhibit lower diffusion-controlled strain rates than multilayers without tungsten.
Tungsten-modified multilayers will exhibit more dislocation-related signatures, including increased dislocation density or slip bands, than controls without tungsten.
HEA multilayers without tungsten interlayers predominantly undergo diffusion-mediated creep at lower temperatures.
HEA multilayers without tungsten interlayers exhibit earlier creep-related deformation under equivalent conditions.
The proposed transition occurs only while tungsten remains microstructurally stable and the interface remains coherent.
At excessively high temperatures, interface decohesion or tungsten instability may cause a reversion to uncontrolled diffusion creep.
